source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts - cost table
finding: Search costs more than a single chain but less than brute-force sampling, and it beat the sampling baselines at similar token cost on Game of 24.
numbers: Game of 24, GPT-4: IO best-of-100 $0.13/case, 33%; CoT best-of-100 $0.47, 49%; ToT $0.74, 74%. ToT used about 5.5k completion tokens vs 6.7k for 100 CoT trials. Creative Writing: ToT about 5x the tokens and money of CoT. Authors: cost can be 5 to 100 times CoT.
limits: One model and one clean task. Cost depends heavily on prompts and search algorithm. Prices are 2023 GPT-4 prices.
agent_relevance: Search must be compared with best-of-N at equal tokens (guardrail G7). Here it wins on a task with a checkable end state.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts - model ablation
finding: Most of the Game of 24 gain depends on the model that proposes thoughts; evaluating states is easier than generating them.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-3.5 IO 6%, CoT 3%, ToT 19%; GPT-4 IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, ToT 74%. GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%; GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. A 3-shot proposal prompt was needed for GPT-3.5.
limits: 100 games. Single run per cell, no confidence intervals reported.
agent_relevance: A cheap model may judge states while a strong model proposes them. The state-evaluator slot could use a smaller model.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts - mini crosswords ablation
finding: In a deeper search (up to 10 steps) the pruning and backtracking operators carried the gain; the state evaluator was imperfect.
numbers: 5x5 crosswords, 20 test games, GPT-4. Letter/word/game success: IO 38.7/14/0; CoT 40.6/15.6/1; ToT 78/60/20 (4 of 20 games); ToT with oracle best state 82.4/67.5/35 (7 of 20); no pruning 65.4/41.5/5; no backtracking 54.6/20/5. DFS capped at 100 steps.
limits: Tiny test set (20). The evaluator pruned states that were actually correct when words were rare. Without pruning it still solved 4/20, 3 of which pruned ToT missed.
agent_relevance: Backtracking and pruning matter, but only if the evaluator is trusted. A wrong prune is unrecoverable, so prune only on a code check.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts - easy tasks
finding: On tasks GPT-4 already does well, search adds little; it pays only where plain reasoning fails.
numbers: Zero-shot ToT (5 strategies, vote, 5 solutions, vote), 100 random items, GPT-4: GSM8K IO 51, CoT 86, ToT 90; StrategyQA IO 73, CoT 82, ToT 83. Creative writing: GPT-4 coherence score IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56; humans preferred ToT over CoT in 41 of 100 pairs, CoT over ToT in 21, 38 similar.
limits: Creative writing is scored by GPT-4 itself, which our guardrails G5 and G8 distrust. Subsets of 100.
agent_relevance: Gate search on a failed or disagreeing first pass (G1). Do not run it by default on easy items.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP) - Blocksworld
finding: Casting the model as a world model (predict the next state) plus MCTS lifted a small open model above GPT-4 chain-of-thought on planning.
numbers: Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B, success for 2/4/6-step problems: RAP(10) 1.00/0.86/0.26; RAP(20) 1.00/0.88/0.42, average 64%; GPT-4 CoT 0.50/0.63/0.40 (RAP 33% relative gain); CoT pass@10 0.23/0.07/0.00.
quote: allows LLaMA-33B to outperform GPT-4 by 33% relative gain
limits: Small test sets. Best setting used a task-specific reward (goal progress). Blocksworld has a simple simulator form, so model-as-world-model is easy to check.
agent_relevance: This is the Newell and Simon problem space with the model supplying operator effects. Keeping an explicit state and giving each step only the current state is the main trick.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP) - math, logic and rewards
finding: Gain on reasoning tasks is smaller than on planning; the best reward mix depends on the task.
numbers: GSM8K (LLaMA-33B): CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP 48.8 (single trace), RAP-Aggregate about +3. PrOntoQA: answer accuracy 94.2, proof accuracy 78.8 vs CoT proof 64.8 (+14) and CoT+SC prediction (+4.4). Blocksworld: action likelihood + task reward beats single rewards; adding self-evaluation helps slightly. On GSM8K action likelihood hurt with more iterations; self-evaluation was best.
limits: SC gap on GSM8K is only 2 points, so an equal-compute comparison is close. Reward design is needed per task.
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation helps where errors are easier to spot than to avoid (math), not where steps are formulaic (blocks). Fits G2: check against real output where it exists.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP) - full Blocksworld, Llama-2 70B
finding: On the full benchmark, CoT collapses with plan length while search holds up longer, but still declines.
numbers: Easy split success by plan length (CoT / RAP10): 2-step .49/1.00, 4-step .18/.99, 6-step .06/.75, 8-step .01/.61, 10-step .01/.32; overall CoT .08 vs RAP .65. Hard split overall CoT .05 vs RAP .51.
limits: RAP(10) means 10 MCTS iterations, so many more model calls than one chain; calls per case not reported.
agent_relevance: Gains grow with depth, which is where the problem-space framing should be used first.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS) - comparison tables
finding: Adding MCTS plus environment feedback and reflection beat ToT and RAP on reasoning, code and web tasks.
numbers: GPT-3.5 HotpotQA EM, reasoning only: base .32, CoT .34, CoT-SC .38, ToT .55, RAP .60, LATS(CoT) .62. With acting: ReAct .32, best-of-k .38, Reflexion .51, ToT(ReAct) .39, RAP(ReAct) .54, LATS(ReAct) .63, LATS(n=10) .65, LATS(CoT+ReAct) .71. HumanEval GPT-4 pass@1: base 80.1, Reflexion 91.0, LATS 92.7; GPT-3.5: ToT 54.4, RAP 63.1, LATS 83.8. WebShop score/SR: ReAct 53.8/28.0, Reflexion 64.2/35.0, LATS 75.9/38.0.
limits: Part of the gain is external feedback (unit tests, environment). Authors state LATS needs the ability to revert to earlier states.
agent_relevance: Real output (tests, environment) gives search its power. Matches G2 and G3, with the caveat that the HumanEval result may be fitted to visible tests.

source: Zhou et al. (2024) Language Agent Tree Search (LATS) - ablations and cost
finding: Principled search (select, backpropagate) and the model-scored value function mattered; pruned DFS lost a lot.
numbers: HotpotQA: swapping MCTS for DFS with ToT-style pruning dropped EM by .21 (to .42); no LM heuristic .37. At k=50 trajectories: ToT .49, RAP .54, LATS .61 with nodes expanded on success ToT 84.05, RAP 70.60, LATS 66.65. At k=10: ToT .34, RAP .44, LATS .44. Game of 24 GPT-3.5, n=5, k=30: CoT .08, Reflexion .12, ToT .20, RAP .40, LATS(CoT) .44.
limits: Sample complexity is the same O(kn) as ToT and RAP; lower node count is on one task. ToT .20 with GPT-3.5 agrees with the ToT paper's 19%.
agent_relevance: Search design choices change results by 20+ points, so a naive search can look worse than a good one at equal cost. Test the search policy itself.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks - autonomous planning
finding: Models alone produce few valid plans; obfuscating names (same state space, new surface) collapses them, which supports the claim that representation drives performance.
numbers: GPT-4 about 12% of plans executable and goal-reaching in the authors' earlier tests. The 2024 table (GPT-4o, GPT-4-Turbo, Claude-3-Opus, LLaMA-3 70B, Gemini Pro, 600 instances) shows plain Blocksworld in the tens of percent and Mystery Blocksworld (deceptive names) at 0 to 2.5% in the hardest rows. I could not align every table cell from the extracted text.
limits: Table text was garbled, so only coarse ranges are stated. The authors advocate a position.
agent_relevance: Same problem space, renamed objects, collapses accuracy. Test the agent on renamed isomorphs (Simon and Hayes style) to see whether it reasons or recalls.

source: Kambhampati et al. (2024) LLMs Can't Plan, But Can Help Planning in LLM-Modulo Frameworks - verifier loop and ToT critique
finding: An external sound verifier in a generate-test loop works; self-critique does not. The authors argue ToT gets its power from the checker, not from search.
numbers: Blocksworld with VAL back-prompting: 82% within 15 rounds; Logistics 70%; Mystery Blocksworld about 10%. Graph coloring: self-critique no better than direct, and worse because the model discards correct answers it generated by luck.
quote: there is really no deeper connection to search-based agents
limits: Position paper; the ToT claim is an argument, not a controlled test. ToT's Game of 24 has an easily coded verifier.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2, G3, G5: code verifier first, model proposes. Also shows how little remains when the model cannot even propose in a renamed domain.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? (o1 on PlanBench) - accuracy
finding: A reasoning-trained model jumped far above plain LLMs on Blocksworld but lost much of it under renaming and long plans.
numbers: 600 Blocksworld problems: best plain LLM LLaMA 3.1 405B 62.6%; o1-preview 97.8% (o1-mini 56.6%). Mystery Blocksworld o1-preview 52.8%, Randomized Mystery Blocksworld 37.3% (earlier LLMs near 0). Fast Downward planner 100% at far lower cost.
limits: Preliminary evaluation; o1 internals closed; cost per call not controlled.
agent_relevance: Training for long reasoning chains replaces some external search but is brittle to renaming. The scaffold should still test with renamed variants.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? (o1 on PlanBench) - length and unsolvable cases
finding: o1 degrades with plan length and does not say when a problem is unsolvable.
numbers: 110 problems needing 20-40 step plans: o1-preview 23.63%. Unsolvable instances: 27% correctly flagged, 19% empty plan, 54% a full impossible plan; randomized mystery: 16% flagged, 5% empty, 79% impossible plan; 11.5% of solvable instances wrongly called impossible.
limits: Single model, single benchmark family.
agent_relevance: A search agent needs a code-checked way to report no-solution instead of inventing a plan.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning - prompt specificity
finding: Step-by-step example prompts help only when they match the exact problem class; a more general algorithm prompt gives much less.
numbers: 261 table-to-stack Blocksworld instances, accuracy GPT-4-Turbo / Claude-3-Opus / GPT-4: zero-shot 19.1/9.96/3.83; zero-shot CoT 21/10.34/4.98; general n-shot 13.7/16.4/6.13; progression-proof CoT 15.3/4.59/6.89; Blocksworld universal algorithm 37.1/37.1/51.3; problem-class n-shot 18/15.7/8.81; stacking prompt 40.6/24.5/59.3. Self-consistency on these prompts lowered performance.
limits: Very simple problems; three models, now deprecated.
agent_relevance: A scaffold prompt works only in the range its examples cover. Do not claim a general problem-space prompt gives general planning.

source: Stechly, Valmeekam, Kambhampati (2024) Chain of Thoughtlessness? An Analysis of CoT in Planning - scaling with problem size
finding: Gains from specific prompts shrink as the stack grows past the examples; a sound planner stays at 100%.
numbers: Fast Downward 100% on all tested problems. The stacking-prompt gain deteriorates as stack size n passes the size shown. Scalable variants of three other CoT domains showed the same failure pattern. Authors conclude CoT gains are pattern matching, not algorithm learning.
limits: Authors' interpretation; others find in-context algorithm learning is partial.
agent_relevance: Use a code executor for any operator that must scale; do not ask the model to execute long algorithmic sequences.

source: Sel et al. (2024) Algorithm of Thoughts
finding: Putting a search trace itself into one in-context prompt matched ToT with one query instead of about 100.
numbers: Game of 24: IO 7.3% (1 query), CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0% (100 queries), IO+refine 27% (10 queries), ToT b=5 69% (109.1 queries, about 5,500 completion tokens), AoT 71% (1 query, about 1,000 completion tokens). AoT with manual resolution 78%; 9% of AoT failures were running out of tokens. Mini crosswords word success: IO 14%, CoT-SC 15.6%, ToT 46.5% (over 200 queries), AoT 52% (2 queries).
limits: Authors re-ran ToT (69% vs 74% in the original). In-context search is bounded by context length and the model must keep the search state straight.
agent_relevance: One-pass algorithmic traces are a low-cost alternative to controller-driven search, but a code controller keeps the search honest.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through the Lens of Efficiency - results
finding: Use the model once to write the successor function and goal test as code, then run ordinary search; this solved four benchmark sets completely.
numbers: GPT-4 produced the successor function in 1.2 interactions on average and the goal test in 1 for Game of 24; BFS then solved 1361/1361 solvable instances and flagged the 1 unsolvable (100%), in 1.92 to 6.83 s total for all 1362 problems (ToT reported 75% on 100 medium problems). Crosswords: 20/20 games, 5.5 to 346 s; BlocksWorld 502 tasks 100%; PrOntoQA 4000 questions 100%, 2.16 to 2.53 s.
limits: Human feedback was used to fix code; crossword candidate answers were assumed given; no learned heuristic yet.
agent_relevance: Best fit with our design: the model writes the problem space (states, operators, goal test) once; the program searches. This is the Newell and Simon formulation step done by the model, search done by code.

source: Katz et al. (2024) Thought of Search: Planning with Language Models Through the Lens of Efficiency - cost audit
finding: Popular LLM-search methods are neither sound nor complete and are expensive in model calls.
numbers: Estimated cost with GPT-4-turbo (500 input, 50 output tokens per call): IO/CoT about $40, ReAct/ReWOO about $200, RAP about $14,000, LATS about $16,000 across the four datasets. BlocksWorld: 50,143 expansions would need about 14 days and over $1000 if each were an LLM call. ToT with a bound of 100 expansions calls the LLM about 200 times worst case per crossword game.
limits: Estimates, not measured runs; assumes one call per expansion; input length ignored.
agent_relevance: Report model calls per item for every search variant. Counting is done in code anyway.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking - three regimes
finding: On controllable puzzles, thinking models beat plain models only in the middle range; both fail at high size, and thinking effort drops near the cliff.
numbers: Tower of Hanoi, Checker Jumping, River Crossing, Blocks World. Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking vs non-thinking and DeepSeek R1 vs V3: plain model matches or wins at low complexity, thinking wins at medium, both near 0 at high; Hanoi collapse near 8 disks (255 moves). Reasoning tokens rise and then fall near the threshold despite spare budget. Temperature 0 did not change collapse.
limits: Output-length limits and unsolvable River Crossing instances confound it (see Lawsen). One-shot full-trace format for all.
agent_relevance: Low-difficulty items: plain pass is as good as search (supports gating, G1). The cliff is where code execution must take over.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking - given the algorithm
finding: Giving the model the exact Hanoi and Checker Jumping algorithm did not move the collapse point.
numbers: Hanoi and Checker Jumping with the algorithm in the prompt: collapse at roughly the same N as without. Claude 3.7 thinking first error: around move 100 for Hanoi N=10 vs move 4 for River Crossing N=3 (11-move solution). Hanoi N=5 (31 moves) near-perfect; River Crossing N=3 fails.
limits: One model analysed for failure positions; authors read this as training-data familiarity. Lawsen disputes the setup.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the model to execute long prescribed move lists; the program must hold the state and apply operators.

source: Shojaee et al. (2025) The Illusion of Thinking - trace analysis
finding: Within one trace, correct answers appear early on easy items and later on medium ones; on hard items they never appear.
numbers: Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking traces. Hanoi N=1-4: accuracy declines over the trace (overthinking); N=5-7: slight rise with continued reasoning; N>=8: near-zero throughout. Same pattern across puzzles.
limits: One model; treats the trace as a faithful record, which our schema warns against.
agent_relevance: Suggests stop-and-verify early on easy items and hand over to code search when progress stalls.

source: Lawsen (2025) Comment on The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Much of the reported collapse is a setup artifact: output-length limits and unsolvable River Crossing instances.
numbers: Full Hanoi move list needs about 10 tokens per move (corrected from 5), so output grows with the 2^N-1 moves; with a 64k limit N near 7-8 is the ceiling. River Crossing with N>=6 actors and boat capacity 3 has no solution, so scoring them as failures is wrong. Asked for a generating function instead of a move list, preliminary runs on Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Claude Opus 4, OpenAI o3 and Gemini 2.5 gave very high accuracy in under 5,000 tokens.
quote: Models receive zero scores not for reasoning failures, but for correctly recognizing unsolvable problems.
limits: Preliminary, few runs, no count table. The paper itself notes AI co-authorship.
agent_relevance: Representation matters: asking for a program (a compact operator) instead of a long trace removes the collapse. Favours code-as-operator.

source: Varela et al. (2025) Rethinking the Illusion of Thinking
finding: Replicating Hanoi and River Crossing with stepwise prompting and two-model dialogue: output limits explain part but not all of the Hanoi failure; solvable River Crossing is easy.
numbers: Gemini models. Hanoi N=3 to 10, 10 trials each. Stepwise prompting (p moves per sub-stage) delayed collapse, but failures still began near N=8. Two-model dialogue did worse, struggling from N=4 and looping without illegal moves. River Crossing, solvable configurations only: models solved instances with over 100 actor-agent pairs.
limits: Gemini only; plots read approximately; 10 trials per cell.
agent_relevance: Chunking the move sequence helps; adding a second chatting model did not (consistent with G4).

source: Su et al. (2025) Limits of Emergent Reasoning of LLMs in Agentic Frameworks for Deterministic Games
finding: Giving the model an environment interface that tracks state (one tool call per move) did not remove the Hanoi collapse and made it start earlier.
numbers: Hanoi up to n=8 disks; Claude 3.7 Sonnet (with and without thinking), DeepSeek V3.1 and R1. Baseline one-shot: near-zero past a threshold, thinking models better but still collapse. Agentic: collapse at lower n than baseline; at n=8 about 40% of the time the model deterministically reused earlier continuations; loop rate rose with n; policy diverged from both optimal and uniform-random policies.
limits: Small-team preprint; exact success numbers are only in figures.
agent_relevance: Code-held state is not enough. A program that detects repeated states must interrupt the model, as our impasse detector does.

source: Utsho et al. (2026) Complexity-Induced Limits in LLMs on Finite Discrete State-Space Problems
finding: Nine parameterized puzzles with deterministic validators show a sharp drop past task-specific size thresholds even for 2026 frontier reasoning models; longer reasoning does not reliably help.
numbers: Tasks: SAT, cryptarithmetic, graph coloring, River Crossing, Tower of Hanoi, Water Jug, Checker Jumping, Sudoku, Rubik's Cube. Models include GPT-5 Pro, Gemini 3 Pro Preview, Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen Plus, Kimi K2 Thinking. Accuracy drops often exceed 50% past threshold; at Hanoi level 4 every model except Gemini 3 Pro and DeepSeek V3.2 collapses; GPT-5 Pro best overall; gains in one family do not transfer.
limits: Preprint; thresholds follow the authors' level definitions; I did not check per-cell numbers.
agent_relevance: The cliff persists in 2026 models, so the code-side search layer is still needed beyond a size. Measure the collapse point per task type as a routing rule.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search (SoS)
finding: Training a small model on full search traces (including dead ends and backtracking) beat training on only the optimal path, and further RL solved problems the symbolic solvers could not.
numbers: Countdown, 4 input numbers, targets 10 to 100. SoS-pretrained model 51.27% on held-out inputs vs 25.73% for the optimal-path model (+25 points); fine-tuned with STaR or APA it solves 36% of previously unsolved problems; APA gives about 6% overall gain. Only about 57% of generated trajectories reach the solution.
limits: Training, not a scaffold; small model from scratch on one task.
agent_relevance: We do not train, but this supports showing search steps (including failures) in context rather than only the final path; test as a trace format.

source: Wray, Kirk, Laird (2024) Eliciting Problem Specifications via Large Language Models
finding: Soar researchers used an LLM agent to write the problem-space spec (states, operators, goal, illegal states) from a natural-language task, then let a Soar agent search it with weak methods.
numbers: Prompts follow Newell's (1980) problem-space definition and Polya's How to Solve It. Water jug family, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (0125-preview), temperature 0.6, one run per condition, total API cost about $3. For familiar jug cases one-shot CoT gave correct specs; for the mixed-unit variant (4 quart vs 9 gallon) the CoT solver noticed the mismatch but did not use it, while the multi-node analyst agent defined the state with units correctly and Soar search succeeded. GPT-3.5 specs were imprecise (illegal initial state); GPT-4 was needed.
limits: Feasibility study: one problem family, no statistics; search-control and test-case nodes were weaker.
agent_relevance: Direct old-meets-new case: the model formulates the space, a classical architecture searches it. Supports the Thought of Search design; the critique-and-refine node helped.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) NL2GenSym: Natural Language to Generative Symbolic Rules for SOAR via LLMs
finding: An LLM generator plus a critic that tests rules by running them in Soar raised the rate of correct rule generation from natural language on water-jug problems.
numbers: Water Jug Problem dataset, Gemini and Qwen models. Abstract: success rate over 86%, more than 25 points above one-shot overall, hard cases up 56.67 points with Gemini. Ablations reduced success by 14 to 37 points.
limits: Single puzzle family, authors' own dataset; several table cells garbled in extraction so only abstract and prose figures are used.
agent_relevance: Execution-grounded generator and critic (run it, show the failing output) matches G2. A model-only critic would not be enough.

source: Ishay and Lee (2025) LLM+AL: Bridging LLMs and Action Languages
finding: Missionaries-and-Cannibals elaborations and Hanoi variants defeated plain models; having the model write a formal action description for a solver did better.
numbers: Table 1 has 17 problems (14 solvable). Missionaries and Cannibals elaborations: Claude 3 Opus and Gemini 1.0 Ultra solved none, ChatGPT-4 3, o1-preview 7, LLM+AL (o1-preview writes the BC+ program) 7 automatically, the rest after about 3.1 manual corrections. Hanoi variations: ChatGPT-4 solved 1, o1-preview 2. 89.7% (35 of 39) of ChatGPT-4's rule violations came in the first three steps. Self-revision raised executable programs from 22.3% (7/30) to 86.7% (26/30) and correct answers from 16.6% to 50%.
limits: Small number of puzzles (30 across two tables); human corrections used; 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Small rule changes (isomorph-like elaborations) break plain models. Self-revision from solver errors helps, which fits G2.

source: Wu et al. (2023) SmartPlay: A Benchmark for LLMs as Intelligent Agents
finding: Even in a 3-disk Tower of Hanoi interactive game, LLM agents lose track of intermediate states and trail humans.
numbers: Hanoi3Disk, scores normalized to human: GPT-4 variants lead other LLMs but stay below humans; authors report about a 10% gap to humans on 3-disk Hanoi (vs 40% on Minecraft creative tasks, 70% on Crafter). Authors note LLMs struggle to memoize intermediate states.
limits: Table cells garbled in extraction; only the prose gap statement is used.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping the state outside the model (code-held) instead of recalling it from context.
